Univariate Calibration Curve

Source: R/calibration_curve.R
calibration_curve.Rd

Fits a univariate calibration curve (signal against concentration), with its figures of merit, limits of detection and quantification, and tests of linearity. The curve predicts the concentration of new samples from their signal, with confidence intervals.

Usage

calibration_curve(
  data,
  signal,
  concentration,
  model = "linear",
  weights = NULL,
  blank = NULL,
  lod_method = NULL,
  level = 0.95,
  regression = "ols",
  concentration_se = NULL,
  signal_se = NULL,
  variance_ratio = NULL,
  lod_convention = "ich",
  alpha = 0.05,
  beta = 0.05,
  replicates = 1
)

Arguments

data

A data frame with the calibration samples.

signal, concentration

The columns of data holding the signal and the reference concentration, unquoted or as strings.

model

"linear" (default) or "quadratic".

weights

NULL (default, unweighted), "1/x", "1/x2", or a numeric vector of weights, one per row of data.

blank

An optional numeric vector of replicate signals of a blank sample.

lod_method

The estimate of the blank standard deviation: "residual", "intercept" or "blank" (see details). By default, "blank" when blank is given, "residual" otherwise.

level

The confidence level of the intervals of the coefficients. Default is 0.95.

regression

"ols" (default, least squares), "deming" or "york" (see details).

concentration_se, signal_se

For regression = "york" or "deming": the columns of data with the standard uncertainties of the concentration and of the signal of each standard, unquoted or as strings.

variance_ratio

For regression = "deming": the ratio of the error variance of the signal to that of the concentration. By default, it is computed from signal_se and concentration_se.

lod_convention

The convention of the limits of detection and quantification: "ich" (default, \(3.3\,\sigma/S\) and \(10\,\sigma/S\)) or "iso11843" (ISO 11843-2 and IUPAC; see details).

alpha, beta

For lod_convention = "iso11843": the probabilities of false positives and of false negatives. Default is 0.05.

replicates

For lod_convention = "iso11843": the number of replicate measurements averaged for a sample. Default is 1.

Value

An object of class specproc_calibration, a list with

  • coefficients: a tibble of the estimates, standard errors and confidence intervals (lower, upper) at level;

  • figures_of_merit: a tibble with the number of standards n, the sensitivity, r_squared, the residual standard deviation sigma, the blank standard deviation used (sigma_blank), the critical_value (ISO 11843 only, NA otherwise), lod and loq (in concentration units);

  • linearity: a tibble with the statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value of Mandel's test and of the lack-of-fit test (when they apply);

  • fit: the least-squares lm fit, eiv, the Deming or York fit (NULL for least squares), with its chi_squared, and data, the calibration data.

Use predict() for new samples and plot_calibration() to draw the curve.

Details

The signal, such as a line intensity from line_intensities() or a line ratio, is modeled as a straight line or a second-degree polynomial of the concentration, fitted by (weighted) least squares. Weights "1/x" or "1/x2" suit signals whose variance grows with concentration, which is common in LIBS.

Figures of merit. The sensitivity is the slope of the curve at zero concentration. The limits of detection and quantification are \(LOD = 3.3\,\sigma / S\) and \(LOQ = 10\,\sigma / S\) (ICH, 2005), where \(S\) is the sensitivity and \(\sigma\) the standard deviation of the signal of a blank, estimated from

  • "residual": the residual standard deviation of the fit (default without blank);

  • "intercept": the standard error of the intercept;

  • "blank": the standard deviation of replicate blank signals (default when given).

With weights, the residual standard deviation depends on the scale of the weights, so prefer "blank" or "intercept".

With lod_convention = "iso11843", the limits follow ISO 11843-2 and IUPAC (Currie, 1999), and account for the uncertainty of the curve and for the false positive and false negative risks \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). The standard deviation of a net signal near zero is \(\sigma_0 = \sqrt{\sigma^2 / K + s_a^2}\), where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the signal ("residual" or "blank"), \(K\) the number of replicates averaged for a sample and \(s_a\) the standard error of the intercept. The critical value (decision limit), above which an element is detected, is \(x_C = t_{1-\alpha,\nu}\,\sigma_0 / S\); the limit of detection, the content detected with probability \(1 - \beta\), is \(x_D = \delta_{\nu,\alpha,\beta}\,\sigma_0 / S\), where \(\delta\) is the noncentrality parameter of the noncentral t distribution (about \(2 t_{1-\alpha,\nu}\) for \(\alpha = \beta\)) and \(\nu\) the degrees of freedom of \(\sigma\); and the limit of quantification (IUPAC) is \(x_Q = 10\,\sigma_0 / S\). For a weighted curve, the standard deviation must come from blank signals.

Errors in the concentrations. Least squares assume exact concentrations. When those of the standards are uncertain, such as the certified values of reference materials, the slope is biased toward zero and the intervals too narrow. regression = "york" fits the line by the method of York et al. (2004), with the standard uncertainties of the concentration (concentration_se) and of the signal (signal_se) of each standard; its standard errors are multiplied by the square root of the reduced chi-squared when it exceeds 1 (the points scatter more than their uncertainties explain). regression = "deming" (Deming regression) assumes constant uncertainties, whose ratio variance_ratio (variance of the signal over variance of the concentration, in their units) is given, or computed from the mean squared signal_se and concentration_se; its standard errors come from the scatter of the points. Both fit straight lines without weights; the tests of linearity are those of the least-squares fit.

Linearity. For a straight line, Mandel's test compares its residual variance with that of a quadratic fit; a small p-value means that the curvature is significant (as with self-absorption or detector saturation). When concentrations are replicated, the lack-of-fit test compares the residuals with the pure error of the replicates.

Intervals. The confidence band of the curve shows where the mean signal lies at each concentration; the prediction band, wider, where a single new measurement is expected to fall, since it adds the noise of the measurement. plot_calibration() draws either or both, and predict() computes them for given concentrations (type = "signal").

Inverse prediction. The concentration of a sample is the solution of the calibration equation for its signal (for a quadratic curve, the root within or nearest to the calibration range). Its standard error, by the delta method, combines the uncertainty of the curve with that of the new signal, the mean of replicates measurements.

References

  • Currie, L.A. (1999). Detection and quantification limits: origins and historical overview. Analytica Chimica Acta, 391(2):127-134.

  • ICH (2005). Validation of analytical procedures: text and methodology Q2(R1). International Conference on Harmonisation.

  • ISO 11843-2 (2000). Capability of detection, Part 2: Methodology in the linear calibration case. International Organization for Standardization, Geneva.

  • Mandel, J. (1964). The Statistical Analysis of Experimental Data. Interscience, New York.

  • Miller, J.N., Miller, J.C. (2018). Statistics and Chemometrics for Analytical Chemistry, 7th ed. Pearson, Harlow.

  • York, D., Evensen, N.M., López Martínez, M., De Basabe Delgado, J. (2004). Unified equations for the slope, intercept, and standard errors of the best straight line. American Journal of Physics, 72(3):367-375.

See also

predict.specproc_calibration(), plot_calibration(), line_intensities(), nas()

Author

Christian L. Goueguel

Examples

data(forageLIBS)
# the K I 769.90 nm line, normalized to the C I 247.86 nm line of the matrix
lines <- line_intensities(forageLIBS[-(1:14)], c(C = 247.856, K = 769.896), baseline = TRUE)
standards <- data.frame(
  K = forageLIBS$K,
  signal = lines$intensity[lines$line == "K"] / lines$intensity[lines$line == "C"]
)
cal <- calibration_curve(standards[1:300, ], signal, K)
cal
#> Linear calibration curve (300 standards)
#> 
#>       term estimate std_error  lower  upper
#>  intercept   0.2708   0.03240 0.2070 0.3345
#>      slope   0.1384   0.01556 0.1078 0.1690
#> 
#> R-squared:    0.20976
#> Sensitivity:  0.1384
#> LOD:          3.38  (residual)
#> LOQ:          10.2
#> Mandel:        F = 4.03, p = 0.0457
#> Lack of fit:   F = 1.13, p = 0.239
# the concentrations of new samples, from their signals
head(predict(cal, standards$signal[301:368]))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   signal concentration    se   lower upper below_lod below_loq outside_range
#>    <dbl>         <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <lgl>     <lgl>     <lgl>        
#> 1  0.459          1.36  1.03 -0.665   3.38 TRUE      TRUE      FALSE        
#> 2  0.543          1.97  1.03 -0.0538  3.99 TRUE      TRUE      FALSE        
#> 3  0.580          2.23  1.03  0.212   4.25 TRUE      TRUE      FALSE        
#> 4  0.492          1.59  1.03 -0.427   3.62 TRUE      TRUE      FALSE        
#> 5  0.481          1.52  1.03 -0.507   3.54 TRUE      TRUE      FALSE        
#> 6  0.501          1.67  1.03 -0.355   3.69 TRUE      TRUE      FALSE        

# limits of detection by ISO 11843-2
calibration_curve(standards[1:300, ], signal, K, lod_convention = "iso11843")
#> Linear calibration curve (300 standards)
#> 
#>       term estimate std_error  lower  upper
#>  intercept   0.2708   0.03240 0.2070 0.3345
#>      slope   0.1384   0.01556 0.1078 0.1690
#> 
#> R-squared:    0.20976
#> Sensitivity:  0.1384
#> Critical:     1.73  (ISO 11843, alpha = 0.05)
#> LOD:          3.47  (beta = 0.05; residual)
#> LOQ:          10.5  (IUPAC, 10 sigma)
#> Mandel:        F = 4.03, p = 0.0457
#> Lack of fit:   F = 1.13, p = 0.239

# reference materials with certified values known within 3%, and
# signals within 2% (simulated)
set.seed(1)
crm <- data.frame(certified = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8))
crm$signal <- 0.05 + 0.2 * crm$certified * (1 + rnorm(6, sd = 0.02)) +
  0.2 * rnorm(6, sd = 0.03 * crm$certified)
crm$certified_se <- 0.03 * crm$certified
crm$signal_se <- 0.02 * crm$signal
calibration_curve(crm, signal, certified, regression = "york",
                  concentration_se = certified_se, signal_se = signal_se)
#> Linear calibration curve (6 standards, York regression)
#> 
#>       term estimate std_error   lower  upper
#>  intercept  0.04832  0.005072 0.03424 0.0624
#>      slope  0.20442  0.004422 0.19214 0.2167
#> 
#> R-squared:    0.99835
#> Chi-squared:  0.372 (reduced)
#> Sensitivity:  0.2044
#> LOD:          0.454  (residual)
#> LOQ:          1.38
#> Mandel:        F = 1.86, p = 0.266
